'''Antony John Williams''' is a [[British people|British]] [[chemist]] and expert in the fields of both [[Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy|nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy]] and [[cheminformatics]] at the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]].<ref name="googlescholar">{{GoogleScholar|O2L8nh4AAAAJ}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bio-itworldexpo.com/uploadedFiles/Bio-IT_World_Expo/Agenda/14/2014-BIT-Brochure.pdf|title=2014-BIT-Brochure|last=Staff|website=2014 Bio-IT World Expo|publisher=Cambridge Healthtech Institute|pages=3 (col 2)|access-date=15 June 2016|quote=Antony Williams, Ph.D., Vice President, Strategic Development; Head, Cheminformatics for the Royal Society of Chemistry (RSC)|url-access=registration }}</ref> He is the founder of the [[ChemSpider]] website that was purchased by the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] in May 2009. He is a science blogger<ref>[http://www.chemconnector.com ChemConnector Website]</ref> and an author.<ref>Practical Interpretation of P-31 NMR Spectra and Computer Assisted Structure Verification, Louis Quin and Antony Williams, {{ISBN|978-0-9735913-0-9}}</ref><ref>[http://www.wiley.com/WileyCDA/WileyTitle/productCd-0470638036.html Collaborative Computational Technologies for Biomedical Research], Sean Ekins, Maggie Hupcey and Antony Williams, {{ISBN|978-0-470-63803-3}}</ref><ref name="epmc">{{EuropePMC|ORCID=0000-0002-2668-4821}}</ref><ref>[http://www.linkedin.com/in/AntonyWilliams Antony Williams on LinkedIn.com]</ref><ref>[http://www.mendeley.com/profiles/antony-williams/ Williams' Mendeley Profile]</ref><ref>[http://www.chemconnector.com/chemunicating/ Antony Williams ChemConnector Blog] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110128225341/http://www.chemconnector.com/chemunicating/ |date=January 28, 2011 }}</ref><ref name="scopus">{{Scopus|id=55258539900}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Antony Williams was born in [[St Asaph]], [[Wales]], June 1964 to Ernest Edward Williams, owner of a building contracting firm, and Eirlys Elizabeth Williams. He has one older sister, Rae. He grew up in a small village near [[Caerwys]].

Williams attended Primary School in both [[Holywell, Flintshire|Holywell]] and [[Nannerch]] until 1975. From the age of eleven, he attended [[Alun School]] where he received A-levels in [[mathematics]], [[geography]], and [[chemistry]].

Williams earned his [[Bachelor of Science]] in [[chemistry]] from the [[University of Liverpool]], in 1985, writing an undergraduate dissertation on "Spectroscopic Studies of [[Vitamin E]] Related Systems" where he applied both [[electron paramagnetic resonance]] (EPR) and [[Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy]] (NMR) to the study of [[molecules]] similar in structure to Vitamin E.

Williams earned his [[Ph.D.]] in chemistry, funded by [[Royal Dutch Shell]], from [[Royal Holloway, University of London]] in 1988 and wrote a thesis entitled "High pressure NMR and relaxation studies of alkyl chain systems".<ref name="phd">{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=Antony John|last=Williams |title=High pressure NMR and relaxation studies of alkyl chain systems |publisher=University of Liverpool |date=1988 |url=http://www.theses.com|author-link=Antony John Williams}}{{subscription required}}</ref> He won the Bourne Medal from the University of London for this work and developed a unifying theory for modeling NMR relaxation data to examine the molecular motions of alkyl chains.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Bratt | first1 = P. J. | last2 = Gillies | first2 = D. G. | last3 = Sutcliffe | first3 = L. H. | last4 = Williams | first4 = A. J. | title = NMR relaxation studies of internal motions: A comparison between micelles and related systems | doi = 10.1021/j100370a001 | journal = The Journal of Physical Chemistry | volume = 94 | issue = 7 | pages = 2727 | year = 1990 }}</ref> He also used the Cobalt-59 NMR chemical shift for cobalt (III) hexacyanide as both a temperature and pressure probe.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Gillies | first1 = D. G. | last2 = Sutcliffe | first2 = L. H. | last3 = Williams | first3 = A. J. | title = Variable-temperature high-pressure investigation of the cobalt-59 NMR spectroscopy of aqueous K3\Co(CN)6] | doi = 10.1002/mrc.955 | journal = Magnetic Resonance in Chemistry | volume = 40 | pages = 57–64 | year = 2002 | s2cid = 98518973 }}</ref> During his PhD he developed an interest in personal computers and wrote software programs to fit NMR relaxation data.

Williams continued his work in spectroscopy at the [[National Research Council (Canada)]] using [[EPR spectroscopy]] to perform single-crystal studies of organometallics compounds.

==Career==
In 1991, Williams joined [[Ottawa University]] as their NMR Facility Manager. He continued his personal interests in multinuclear NMR to perform [[2D-NMR]] experiments examining Selenium exchange in mixed-halogen systems.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Milne | first1 = J. | last2 = Williams | first2 = A. J. | doi = 10.1021/ic00048a018 | title = Exchange processes in diselenium and selenium-sulfur dihalides, Se2X2 and SeSX2 (X = Br, Cl). A selenium-77 2D-EXSY study | journal = Inorganic Chemistry | volume = 31 | issue = 22 | pages = 4534 | year = 1992 }}</ref> He also performed [[Isotopes of silicon|Silicon-29]] and [[Isotopes of tellurium|Tellurium-125]] NMR studies.

In 1992 Williams left Canada for [[Rochester, NY]] to work for the [[Eastman Kodak Company]] as their NMR Technology Leader. At Kodak he used his previous experience in studying alkyl chain related systems to study [[micelles]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Antalek | first1 = B. | last2 = Williams | first2 = A. J. | last3 = Garcia | first3 = E. | last4 = Texter | first4 = J. | title = NMR Analysis of Interfacial Structure Transitions Accompanying Electron-Transfer Threshold Transition in Reverse Microemulsions | doi = 10.1021/la00024a014 | journal = Langmuir | volume = 10 | issue = 12 | pages = 4459 | year = 1994 }}</ref> He was involved in the early adoption of [[Liquid Chromatography]]-NMR into the company and in the development of an [[Open Access movement|Open Access]] laboratory for chemists to use roboticized analytical instrumentation to generate data. At Kodak he was part of a three-member team that developed a web-based [[Laboratory information management system]] (LIMS) system called WIMS,<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Brown | first1 = D. | last2 = Williams | first2 = A. | last3 = McLaughlin | first3 = D. | doi = 10.1016/S0165-9936(97)00046-0 | title = Web-based information management system | journal = TrAC Trends in Analytical Chemistry | volume = 16 | issue = 7 | pages = 370 | year = 1997 }}</ref> the Web-based Information Management System and it was the first web-based LIMS system in the world to manage chemical structures and spectral data. He was granted two patents while at Kodak,<ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120720140952/http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO2&Sect2=HITOFF&p=1&u=/netahtml/PTO/search-bool.html&r=2&f=G&l=50&co1=AND&d=PTXT&s1=6,040,129&OS=6,040,129&RS=6,040,129|title=Photographic emulsion having an improved speed. US Patent 6,040,129}}</ref><ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120716234300/http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO2&Sect2=HITOFF&p=1&u=/netahtml/PTO/search-bool.html&r=1&f=G&l=50&co1=AND&d=PTXT&s1=5,576,432&OS=5,576,432&RS=5,576,432|title=Process for the manufacture of dihydropyrimidines, US Patent 5,576,432}}</ref>

In 1997 he started work for a Canadian start-up company, [[Advanced Chemistry Development|Advanced Chemistry Development (ACD/Labs)]] as their senior product manager. He was responsible for managing all [[spectroscopy]], structure drawing and [[IUPAC nomenclature]],<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Williams | first1 = A. | last2 = Yerin | first2 = A. | doi = 10.3390/40900255 | title = The Need for Systematic Naming Software Tools for Exchange of Chemical Information | journal = Molecules | volume = 4 | issue = 9 | pages = 255 | year = 1999 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Williams | first1 = A. | last2 = Yerin | first2 = A. | doi = 10.1201/9781420076509.pt2 | chapter = Automated Identification and Conversion of Chemical Names to Structure-Searchable Information | title = Chemical Information Mining | pages = 21 | year = 2008 | doi-broken-date = 11 July 2025 | isbn = 978-1-4200-7649-3 | url = https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/653815 }}</ref> products.  While in that role the analytical data management software was expanded to include support for [[mass spectrometry]], [[infrared spectroscopy]], [[UV-Vis spectroscopy]], [[chromatography]] and other forms of analytical sciences. While at the company he initiated a hobby project to link together chemistry databases on the web. This project was called [[ChemSpider]]. ChemSpider was formally announced at the Chicago ACS meeting in March 2007 with a database containing over 10 million compounds sourced from [[PubChem]].
In 2007 when he left ACD/Labs he was the Chief Science Officer. He became an independent consultant working with a number of software companies in the cheminformatics domain, such as [[SimBioSys]], and with research organizations to support their cheminformatics efforts. In parallel he continued to develop the ChemSpider platform with a small group of like-minded individuals interested in the development of web-based systems to serve chemists<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Pence | first1 = H. E. | last2 = Williams | first2 = A. | doi = 10.1021/ed100697w | title = ChemSpider: An Online Chemical Information Resource | journal = Journal of Chemical Education | volume = 87 | issue = 11 | pages = 1123 | year = 2010 | bibcode = 2010JChEd..87.1123P }}</ref><ref>Public Compound Databases – How ChemSpider changed the rules making molecules on the web free, Antony J. Williams in Collaborative Computational Technologies for the Life Sciences, Edited by Sean Ekins, Maggie A.Z. Hupcey and Antony J. Williams, Submitted for Publication to Wiley</ref> The site is a [[crowdsourced]] community for chemistry with chemists depositing their structure collections, spectral data and molecular properties. Williams is focused on educating the community as to the issues of data quality associated with internet chemistry databases.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Williams | first1 = A. | title = A perspective of publicly accessible/open-access chemistry databases | doi = 10.1016/j.drudis.2008.03.017 | journal = Drug Discovery Today | volume = 13 | issue = 11–12 | pages = 495–501 | year = 2008 | pmid =  18549975}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Williams | first1 = A. J. | last2 = Ekins | first2 = S. | doi = 10.1016/j.drudis.2011.07.007 | title = A quality alert and call for improved curation of public chemistry databases | journal = Drug Discovery Today | volume = 16 | issue = 17–18 | pages = 747–750 | year = 2011 | pmid =  21871970}}</ref>

In May 2009 the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] announced that it had acquired ChemSpider.<ref>"to fulfill its strategic objective of disseminating knowledge to the chemical community and advancing the chemical sciences"</ref> Williams joined RSC as their Vice President of Strategic Development for ChemSpider.

In May 2015 he joined the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] to work on the development of websites delivering public access to EPA data<ref>[https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2016-07/documents/antony_williams_chemist_in_epas_national_center_for_computational_toxicology.pdf EPA personal profile]</ref> and tools for [[mass spectrometry]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = McEachran| first1 = A. D. | last2 = Sobus| first2 = J. R. | last3 = Williams | first3 = A. J. | doi = 10.1007/s00216-016-0139-z | title = Identifying known unknowns using the US EPA's CompTox Chemistry Dashboard | journal = Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry | pmid=27987027 | volume=409 | issue = 7 | year=2017 | pages=1729–1735| s2cid = 31754962 }}</ref>

Williams has contributed to the world of "Mobile Chemistry"<ref>[http://www.rsc.org/chemistryworld/Issues/2010/May/MobileChemistryChemistryHandsFace.asp A.J. Williams, Mobile Chemistry – Chemistry in Your Hands and In Your Face, Chemistry World, May 2010]</ref> by contributing to the development of ChemMobi, an [[iPhone]] app for accessing millions of chemical compounds and associated data.

Williams is an advocate for [[Open Notebook Science]] and is a judge for the [[Open Notebook Science Challenge]]. He worked with [[Jean-Claude Bradley]] to deliver a web-based game for teaching the interpretation of spectral data utilizing crowdsourced spectroscopy data deposited onto [[ChemSpider]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Bradley | first1 = J. C. | last2 = Lancashire | first2 = R. J. | last3 = Lang | first3 = A. S. D. | last4 = Williams | first4 = A. J. | title = The Spectral Game: Leveraging Open Data and crowdsourcing for education | doi = 10.1186/1758-2946-1-9 | journal = Journal of Cheminformatics | volume = 1 | issue = 1 | pages = 9 | year = 2009 | pmid =  20298527| pmc =3225864 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Open science advocacy==
Williams introduced an [[Open Access journal]], the ChemSpider Journal of Chemistry, and the development team provided novel online markup technology (ChemMANTIS – Markup And Nomenclature Transformation Integrated System) to allow crowdsourced markup of chemistry related terms linked up, where possible, to the ChemSpider database. Williams is a judge for the [[Open Notebook Science Challenge]]. He promotes the use of [[Open Data]], particularly spectral data, publishes in [[Open access (publishing)|Open Access]] journals and is an advocate for [[Open Notebook Science]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Bradley | first1 = J. C. | last2 = Owens | first2 = K. | last3 = Williams | first3 = A. | doi = 10.1038/npre.2008.1505.1 | title = Chemistry Crowdsourcing and Open Notebook Science | journal = Nature Precedings | year = 2008 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Williams is an advocate for freeing pre-clinical data from the pharmaceutical industry on the internet.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Ekins | first1 = S. | last2 = Williams | first2 = A. J. | doi = 10.1039/b917760b | title = Precompetitive preclinical ADME/Tox data: Set it free on the web to facilitate computational model building and assist drug development | journal = Lab on a Chip | volume = 10 | issue = 1 | pages = 13–22 | year = 2010 | pmid =  20024044| url = https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/654057 }}</ref><ref>A.J. Williams, V. Tkachenko, C. Lipinski, A. Tropsha and S. Ekins, Free Online Resources Enabling Crowdsourced, Drug Discovery World Winter 2009/10, 33-39</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Ekins | first1 = S. | last2 = Williams | first2 = A. J. | doi = 10.1016/j.drudis.2010.08.010 | title = When pharmaceutical companies publish large datasets: An abundance of riches or fool's gold? | journal = Drug Discovery Today | volume = 15 | issue = 19–20 | pages = 812–815 | year = 2010 | pmid =  20732447}}</ref> Williams has worked closely with [[Sean Ekins]] to advocate the release of pre-competitive pharmaceutical data to the community. ==Awards and honors==
Williams was the winner of the [[Jim Gray (computer scientist)|Jim Gray]] [[e-Science]] award in 2012 <ref>[http://blogs.msdn.com/b/msr_er/archive/2012/10/10/2012-jim-gray-award-honors-antony-john-williams.aspx Jim Gray eScience Award, Antony Williams]</ref> and the North Carolina American Chemical Society Distinguished Speaker of the Year Award in 2016.<ref>[http://ncacs.sites.acs.org/History/Distinguished%20Speakers%20Award/index.html NC ACS Distinguished Speaker of the Year Award, Antony Williams]</ref>
